words.shortDefinition: Threat modeling taxonomy: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege.
words.simpleDefinition: STRIDE is a six-category checklist that turns the open-ended question 'what could go wrong?' into a structured walk through every type of harm an attacker can cause. Apply it to each element of your data flow diagram and you systematically cover authentication failures, integrity violations, missing audit logs, data leaks, availability attacks, and privilege escalation.
words.longDefinition: STRIDE was developed by Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg at Microsoft in 1999 and became the foundation of Microsoft's Security Development Lifecycle. Each letter maps to a threat category and the security property it violates: Spoofing attacks Authentication; Tampering attacks Integrity; Repudiation attacks Non-repudiation; Information Disclosure attacks Confidentiality; Denial of Service attacks Availability; Elevation of Privilege attacks Authorization. The taxonomy covers the full CIA+AAA space, which is why it produces complete results when applied systematically. STRIDE is most powerful as STRIDE-per-element: for each process, data store, data flow, and external entity in your DFD, the standard matrix identifies which STRIDE categories apply and focuses the analysis. Its weakness is that it identifies threats without ranking them — CVSS or DREAD scoring is needed afterward to prioritize the resulting list. STRIDE is best suited to early-design threat model sessions because it is low-overhead and produces actionable threat statements with minimal training. A STRIDE threat statement takes the form: 'An attacker could [category action] [target element] by [method], causing [impact].' Microsoft's free Threat Modeling Tool automates STRIDE-per-element generation from DFDs drawn in its editor.
words.connector: Think of STRIDE like a six-column inspection checklist that a building inspector runs on every room — each column covers a different type of hazard, and every room gets checked against all six before sign-off.
words.techContext: During our design review for the payment API, we ran STRIDE-per-element on the DFD and identified three Repudiation threats on the order mutation endpoint that had no corresponding audit log entries.
words.exampleSentence: Running STRIDE on the checkout service DFD surfaced an Elevation of Privilege threat we had overlooked: the order status endpoint accepted user-supplied role fields without server-side validation.

  T (Tampering):             MITM modifies the username field in transit

words.etymology: Acronym coined at Microsoft circa 1999 by Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg; adopted into the Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle and popularized in Adam Shostack's Threat Modeling: Designing for Security (2014).

words.shortDefinition: Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis; seven-stage risk-centric threat modeling methodology.
words.simpleDefinition: PASTA anchors threat modeling in business risk rather than technical categories. Its seven stages move from defining what the business values and fears, through decomposing the application, gathering real-world threat intelligence, mapping vulnerabilities to threats, and finally producing a risk-ranked remediation backlog. Where STRIDE asks what could go wrong, PASTA asks what it would cost if it did.
words.longDefinition: PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) was introduced by Tony UcedaVélez and Marco Morana in Risk Centric Threat Modeling (2015). The seven stages are: (1) Define business objectives — what assets must be protected, what regulations apply, what is the business impact of a breach; (2) Define technical scope — infrastructure inventory, network topology, technology stack; (3) Decompose the application — DFDs, use cases, trust levels, entry points; (4) Analyze threats — compile threat intelligence from CVE databases, MITRE ATT&CK, and industry reports; (5) Identify vulnerabilities — map SAST, DAST, and pen-test findings to stage-4 threats; (6) Enumerate and model attacks — build attack trees for high-priority threats and simulate attack paths; (7) Risk and impact analysis — score residual risk with CVSS or a qualitative model and produce a business-justified remediation backlog. PASTA's primary advantage over STRIDE is traceability: every technical finding is connected to a business impact, making it easier to justify security investment to non-technical stakeholders. Its weakness is time — a full PASTA engagement typically takes days or weeks, making it better suited to high-value systems (payment processors, PII stores) than routine feature reviews. Most mature security programs use STRIDE for daily design reviews and reserve PASTA for quarterly deep-dives on critical systems.
words.connector: Think of PASTA like a business case for every security fix: instead of handing engineers a list of threats, it hands the business a prioritized risk register with dollar-denominated impact estimates attached to each item.
words.techContext: The security team used PASTA for the annual review of the payment processing service, producing a risk-ranked backlog where the top item — unencrypted PII in application logs — was justified by a calculated $2.3M regulatory exposure.
words.exampleSentence: The PASTA engagement for our healthcare portal revealed that our highest-risk threat was not the web application itself but the unencrypted nightly database export job, which was outside the original threat modeling scope.

words.shortDefinition: Structured process of identifying assets, threat actors, attack paths, and mitigations before writing code.
words.simpleDefinition: Threat modeling is the practice of systematically thinking through how your system could be attacked — before you build it, not after an incident. A short threat model session produces a DFD, a list of threats by category, and a set of engineering tickets for mitigations. Teams that do this consistently ship fewer vulnerabilities than those that rely solely on post-hoc testing.
words.longDefinition: Threat modeling is a proactive security discipline that answers Adam Shostack's four questions: What are we building? What could go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good job? The process begins with a data flow diagram (DFD) that maps external entities, processes, data stores, data flows, and trust boundaries. Once the DFD is accurate, a structured threat enumeration method — STRIDE, PASTA, or attack trees — is applied to surface threats systematically. Each threat is classified using a risk framework (CVSS, DREAD, or qualitative High/Medium/Low) and assigned a response: mitigate, accept, transfer, or avoid. Every non-accepted threat becomes a backlog item with an owner. Threat modeling cadence matters as much as method: it should be triggered at design time for any new feature touching authentication, authorization, or external data flows; at major architectural changes; and post-incident to update the model with real-world attack paths. Threat-model-as-code tools (pytm, OWASP Threat Dragon) store the DFD and threat list in version control alongside source code, enabling diff-reviewed updates and CI-enforced checks. Security engineers are not required to run threat model sessions — feature engineers and architects can run STRIDE passes themselves with training, with the security team reviewing outputs and escalating complex cases.
words.connector: Think of threat modeling like planning a road trip with a map — you identify the hazards and detours before you start driving, rather than discovering them when you are already lost at midnight.
words.techContext: After adding threat modeling to our design review checklist for all features touching PII, we caught an authorization bypass in the draft API design before any code was written — saving an estimated three-sprint remediation effort.
words.exampleSentence: The 90-minute threat modeling sprint on the new file-sharing feature produced seven threats, two of which were rated High and converted to blocking tickets before any code was merged.

from pytm import TM, Server, Dataflow, Boundary, Actor, Datastore

tm = TM(name="File Share API", description="User file upload and download")

internal = Boundary(name="Internal Network")

file_store = Datastore(name="S3 Bucket", inBoundary=internal, isEncrypted=True)

upload = Dataflow(browser, api_svc, name="Upload",
                  protocol="HTTPS", isEncrypted=True)
store  = Dataflow(api_svc, file_store, name="Store File",
                  protocol="AWS SDK")

tm.process()  # generates DFD + STRIDE threat report

words.shortDefinition: Software Bill of Materials; machine-readable inventory of every component in an application's dependency graph.
words.simpleDefinition: An SBOM lists every open-source library, transitive dependency, their versions, and cryptographic hashes — the ingredient label for your software. When a critical vulnerability like Log4Shell is disclosed, teams with SBOMs can query whether any product is affected in minutes. Without one, they spend days manually searching dozens of repositories.
words.longDefinition: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is a formal, machine-readable record of every component that makes up a software artifact, modeled on manufacturing bills of materials. An SBOM records for each component: its name and version, a Package URL (purl) for cross-ecosystem identification, cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) for integrity verification, the SPDX license identifier, the supplier or origin, and dependency relationships forming the full graph. The two dominant SBOM standards are CycloneDX (OWASP, security-first design with native vulnerability and attestation support) and SPDX (Linux Foundation, ISO/IEC 5962:2021, originally focused on license compliance). The Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, December 2021) illustrated SBOM's operational value: organizations with SBOMs identified affected systems in hours; those without spent days in manual audits. US Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) subsequently mandated SBOM generation for software sold to the federal government, accelerating industry adoption. SBOMs are generated automatically by tools like Syft, cdxgen, and GitHub's dependency submission API and should be produced as a CI artifact on every release, stored alongside the artifact in the registry, and continuously monitored against CVE databases via tools like Dependency-Track or Grype.
words.connector: Think of an SBOM like a restaurant's full allergen menu — when a recall is issued for a specific ingredient, you know immediately which dishes are affected without opening every pot in the kitchen.
words.techContext: We generate a CycloneDX SBOM for every container image in CI using Syft, store it in our artifact registry, and feed it to Dependency-Track for continuous CVE monitoring across all deployed services.
words.exampleSentence: When the critical OpenSSL vulnerability dropped, our SBOM registry let us identify all 23 affected container images within four minutes and begin coordinated patching before any public advisories had named our stack.

codeExample.code:
# GitHub Actions: generate CycloneDX SBOM and upload
jobs:
  sbom:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: Generate SBOM (CycloneDX JSON)
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
        with:
          image: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          format: cyclonedx-json
          output-file: sbom.cyclonedx.json

      - name: Upload SBOM as release asset
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: sbom-${{ github.sha }}
          path: sbom.cyclonedx.json

words.etymology: Borrowed from manufacturing's 'Bill of Materials' (BOM); the 'Software' prefix was popularized by the US NTIA (National Telecommunications and Information Administration) in 2021 guidance documents.

words.shortDefinition: Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts; framework of four levels increasing build-provenance and integrity guarantees.
words.simpleDefinition: SLSA is a graduated security checklist for build pipelines. Level 1 generates a provenance document. Level 2 requires that document to be signed by the build service. Level 3 hardens the build environment against tampering. Level 4 mandates hermetic, reproducible builds with two-party review — the highest practical assurance that an artifact is what the source claims it to be.
words.longDefinition: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, pronounced 'salsa') was developed by Google in 2021 and is now governed by the OpenSSF. It defines four levels of build integrity. SLSA Level 1 requires the build process to generate a provenance document describing how the artifact was built; the document need not be signed. SLSA Level 2 requires the provenance to be signed by the build service (not the developer); source must be version-controlled and builds must run on a hosted platform. SLSA Level 3 requires the build platform itself to be audited and hardened: no human access to individual build jobs, source retained (not mutable), builds run in isolated environments, build instructions defined in source. SLSA Level 4 adds hermetic builds (all inputs declared and resolved, no network access during build), two-party review of all source changes, and reproducible builds (same inputs always produce bit-for-bit identical output). Each level addresses a specific threat: Level 1 documents what was built; Level 2 prevents individual developer compromise; Level 3 prevents build-service compromise; Level 4 prevents even a compromised build platform from injecting malicious code undetected. GitHub Actions supports SLSA Level 2 provenance generation natively via the slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator action. npm, PyPI, and Maven Central are progressively requiring SLSA Level 2 or higher for published packages.
words.connector: Think of SLSA levels like building codes: Level 1 means there is a blueprint; Level 4 means every brick was inspected, every worker was vetted, two supervisors signed off, and the structure was independently measured to match the plans.
words.techContext: After the dependency confusion incident, our security team mandated SLSA Level 2 compliance for all first-party services, requiring signed provenance attestations alongside every container image pushed to production.
words.exampleSentence: Adopting SLSA Level 2 meant that our deployment system could cryptographically verify each image was built from our official GitHub repository and not from a fork or a compromised developer machine.

codeExample.code:
# SLSA Level 2 provenance via slsa-github-generator
jobs:
  build:
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.hash.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build binary
        run: go build -o myapp .
      - name: Hash artifact
        id: hash
        run: echo "digest=$(sha256sum myapp | base64 -w0)" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

  provenance:
    needs: [build]
    uses: slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/.github/workflows/generator_generic_slsa3.yml@v2.0.0
    with:
      base64-subjects: ${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}

words.etymology: Acronym for Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts; deliberately pronounceable as 'salsa' for memorability; introduced by Google in 2021 and now hosted under the OpenSSF.

words.shortDefinition: Open-source toolchain for keyless signing and verification of software artifacts using ephemeral certificates.
words.simpleDefinition: Sigstore solves the key management problem that caused most teams to skip artifact signing entirely. Developers authenticate with an OIDC provider (GitHub Actions, Google), receive a 10-minute signing certificate, sign the artifact, and discard the key. The signing event is logged permanently to a public transparency ledger called Rekor. Anyone can verify the signature by checking the ledger.
words.longDefinition: Sigstore is an OpenSSF project (sigstore.dev) initiated by Google, Red Hat, and Purdue University in 2021. It has three core components. Fulcio is a certificate authority that issues short-lived (10-minute) code-signing certificates to callers who authenticate via OIDC — a GitHub Actions workflow, a Google account, or a Microsoft identity. The certificate embeds the caller's identity as the subject. After signing, the private key is discarded. Rekor is an immutable, append-only transparency log backed by a Merkle tree; every signing event is recorded with the certificate, artifact digest, and timestamp and cannot be deleted or altered without detection. Cosign is the CLI and Go library for signing artifacts, verifying signatures, attaching attestations (SBOM, vulnerability scan results, SLSA provenance), and querying Rekor. The keyless flow: authenticate with OIDC → Fulcio issues ephemeral cert → sign the artifact → log the event to Rekor → discard the private key. Verification: locate the Rekor entry → verify the cert chain → verify the signature. No long-lived key material is required. Sigstore was adopted by PyPI in 2023 for package provenance, by npm experimentally in 2023, and GitHub Artifact Attestations (2024) builds directly on Sigstore infrastructure. The result is that artifact signing has gone from a rarely-used operational burden to a routine CI step.
words.connector: Think of Sigstore like a public notary office that never closes: you prove your identity at the counter, the notary witnesses you sign the document, records the event in a permanent ledger, and you walk away without keeping a copy of your stamp.
words.techContext: Our CI pipeline uses Sigstore keyless signing via Cosign to sign every container image with the GitHub Actions workflow identity, allowing our Kubernetes admission controller to reject any image lacking a valid signature from our official build system.
words.exampleSentence: After integrating Sigstore, our images are signed with the GitHub Actions workflow identity — giving us cryptographic proof of build provenance without storing any private keys in CI secrets.

# Keyless Sigstore signing in GitHub Actions
- name: Sign container image

    COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL: "1"   # enables keyless mode
  run: |
    cosign sign --yes \
      ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

# Verification command (in deployment gate):
# cosign verify \
#   --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/myorg/myrepo' \
#   --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' \
#   <image-ref>

words.etymology: Portmanteau of 'signature' + 'store'; an OpenSSF project originally initiated by Google, Red Hat, and Purdue University and publicly launched in 2021.

words.shortDefinition: Sigstore tool for signing and verifying container images and OCI artifacts against a transparency log.
words.simpleDefinition: Cosign is the CLI at the center of the Sigstore ecosystem. It signs container images using either a private key you manage or Sigstore's keyless OIDC flow, stores signatures in the same OCI registry as the image, and verifies signatures by confirming that the signing identity matches an expected workflow or key. Kubernetes admission controllers use Cosign's library to enforce 'only signed images from approved sources run here'.
words.longDefinition: Cosign (github.com/sigstore/cosign, maintained by the Linux Foundation) is the primary tool for container image and OCI artifact signing. Signatures are stored as OCI artifacts in the same registry as the image using the :sha256-<digest>.sig tag convention, meaning signatures travel with images and no separate signature distribution infrastructure is needed. Cosign supports three signing modes: keyless (Sigstore OIDC flow via Fulcio, recommended for CI), KMS-based (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault), and traditional key-based (cosign.key file). Beyond signing images, Cosign can attach attestations — SBOM documents, SLSA provenance, vulnerability scan results — to images via cosign attest, using the in-toto attestation specification. cosign verify-attestation retrieves and checks these policy assertions. In Kubernetes, the sigstore policy-controller, Kyverno, and Connaisseur use Cosign's verification library as an admission webhook: when a pod is scheduled, the controller verifies that the image has a valid signature from the expected identity before allowing it to start. This enforces a hard 'no unsigned image runs in production' policy without manual review. cosign verify accepts --certificate-identity-regexp and --certificate-oidc-issuer flags, allowing policy writers to assert that an image must have been signed by a specific GitHub Actions workflow from a specific repository.
words.connector: Think of Cosign like a wax seal on a letter — before opening the container, the admission controller checks that the seal matches the expected sender's stamp, proving it was not switched in transit.
words.techContext: Our Kubernetes clusters run the sigstore policy-controller, which calls Cosign to verify that every image deployed to production was signed by our GitHub Actions release workflow before the pod is admitted.
words.exampleSentence: After integrating Cosign into our admission controller, a compromised third-party image lacking a valid signature was rejected at the cluster boundary before any workload could instantiate it.

codeExample.code:
# Sign an image after push (keyless, GitHub Actions identity)
cosign sign --yes \
  ghcr.io/myorg/myapp@sha256:abc123...

# Verify before deployment
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity \
    'https://github.com/myorg/myapp/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer \
    'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' \
  ghcr.io/myorg/myapp:latest

# Attach a CycloneDX SBOM attestation
cosign attest \
  --predicate sbom.cyclonedx.json \
  --type cyclonedx \
  ghcr.io/myorg/myapp@sha256:abc123...

words.etymology: Co-sign in the financial sense means to jointly sign a document as a guarantor; in the Sigstore ecosystem the tool co-signs container images alongside their content digest using an OIDC-bound certificate.

words.shortDefinition: Attack registering a public package with the same name as an internal one, tricking package managers into fetching it.
words.simpleDefinition: If your company uses a private package named 'company-utils' at version 1.2.3, an attacker can publish 'company-utils' version 9.9.9 to npm or PyPI. Package managers that check both registries will prefer the higher version number on the public registry, silently installing the malicious package during your next npm install — including in CI.
words.longDefinition: Dependency confusion (also called namespace confusion) was documented by security researcher Alex Birsan in February 2021 in a paper that demonstrated the attack against Apple, Microsoft, Tesla, Shopify, Uber, Yelp, and PayPal simultaneously. The attack exploits how multi-registry package manager configurations resolve names: when both a private registry and the public registry contain a package with the same name, most package managers default to installing the higher version number. An attacker registers the target's internal package name on the public registry with an artificially inflated version (e.g., 9.9.9) and embeds a malicious postinstall script that executes during npm install or pip install, exfiltrating environment variables containing CI secrets, cloud credentials, or developer machine data. The attack required no social engineering and succeeded entirely through a design flaw in registry resolution logic. Mitigations include: using scoped npm package names (@company/utils) that cannot be claimed on the public registry; configuring package managers to use registry-exclusive resolution for internal package namespaces; committing lockfiles that pin exact registry origins; and publishing placeholder packages to public registries under internal names to prevent adversarial occupation. Birsan's paper earned him over $130,000 in bug bounties from the affected companies and triggered widespread changes in how organizations configure their artifact proxies.
words.connector: Think of dependency confusion like a restaurant supply attack: someone stocks the public food market with a product labeled 'Chef's Secret Sauce' at a price too good to resist, and the kitchen's automated ordering system buys it instead of the verified private supplier's version.
words.techContext: After Birsan's paper, we audited our Artifactory configuration and found three internal npm packages resolvable from the public registry; we scoped them under @company/ and configured scope-exclusive registry rules within 48 hours.
words.exampleSentence: The dependency confusion attack succeeded because our npm config checked the public registry before the private one — a one-line npmrc change to pin internal scopes to the private registry would have blocked it entirely.

codeExample.code:
# .npmrc: prevent dependency confusion for internal packages
# Route @company scope exclusively to private registry
@company:registry=https://registry.company.internal/npm/

# Alternatively, use pip --index-url to pin Python packages
# pip.ini (or pyproject.toml [tool.pip])
[global]
index-url = https://pypi.company.internal/simple/
extra-index-url = https://pypi.org/simple/
# Note: extra-index-url still allows confusion — prefer exclusive routing
# or use --require-hashes to pin exact content

words.etymology: Coined by Alex Birsan in his February 2021 research paper 'Dependency Confusion: How I Hacked Into Apple, Microsoft and Dozens of Other Companies'; confusion refers to the package manager's inability to distinguish same-named packages across registries.

words.shortDefinition: Malicious package published under a name nearly identical to a popular library, installed when developers mistype.
words.simpleDefinition: A typosquatter registers a package name one character away from a widely-used library — 'reqeusts' for 'requests', 'colourama' for 'colorama' — and waits. Every developer who mistypes during installation unknowingly runs whatever install script the attacker included. Unlike dependency confusion, no internal package name is required; the attacker just needs patience.
words.longDefinition: Typosquatting on package registries exploits the gap between what a developer intended to type and what they actually typed. The attacker registers typographic variants of popular library names and publishes malicious packages that execute code during installation via lifecycle hooks (npm's postinstall, Python's setup.py). Common techniques include character transposition (reqeusts vs. requests), dropped or added characters (colourama — a UK spelling variant — vs. colorama, which was installed 12,000 times before removal in 2021), hyphen/underscore substitution (python-dateutil vs. python_dateutil), and combosquatting (react-native-fast-image-loader targeting react-native-fast-image users). The malicious payload typically exfiltrates environment variables (capturing CI secrets and cloud credentials), installs a backdoor, or serves as a loader for a second-stage payload. In 2022, researchers found over 200 malicious PyPI packages in a single campaign targeting AWS credentials and Discord tokens. PyPI and npm now have automated scanning that detects many typosquatting attempts, but novel variants are published faster than detection keeps pace. Mitigations: commit lockfiles (once the correct package is installed, reinstallation uses the locked version); audit new packages before adding them by checking download counts, repository links, and maintainer profiles; route all package downloads through a private artifact proxy with an approved-packages allowlist.
words.connector: Think of typosquatting like counterfeit products displayed next to the original on a shop shelf, with nearly identical packaging — a customer who grabs the wrong box gets a product that looks right but does something harmful.
words.techContext: After discovering a typosquatted version of our internal UI library on npm with 400 installs, we implemented an Artifactory allowlist that blocks any package not explicitly approved, regardless of name similarity.
words.exampleSentence: The postinstall script in the typosquatted package sent all CI environment variables — including the AWS deployment key — to an external endpoint before the security scanner flagged it four hours later.

words.etymology: Compound of 'typo' (typographical error) + 'squatting' (occupying a name or resource to which one has no legitimate claim); borrowed from the domain name typosquatting practice of registering misspelled domain names.

words.shortDefinition: Static analysis of infrastructure-as-code templates (Terraform, CloudFormation) for misconfigurations before deployment.
words.simpleDefinition: IaC scanning runs security and compliance rules against your Terraform, CloudFormation, Bicep, or Kubernetes manifests before any infrastructure is provisioned. It catches misconfigured S3 buckets, security groups open to the world, unencrypted databases, and privilege escalation risks at PR time — when they cost nothing to fix — rather than in production, where they can cost millions.
words.longDefinition: Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) scanning applies static analysis principles to infrastructure definition files. Tools like Checkov, tfsec, Terrascan, KICS (Keeping Infrastructure as Code Secure), and Snyk IaC evaluate Terraform plans, AWS CloudFormation templates, Azure Bicep files, Kubernetes YAML manifests, and Helm charts against a ruleset of security and compliance checks. Common findings include: S3 buckets with public ACLs, security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports, RDS instances without encryption at rest, IAM roles with wildcard permissions, Kubernetes pods running as root, or container images pulled without digest pinning. Most tools map findings to compliance frameworks (CIS benchmarks, SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA) so that security engineers can report findings in terms auditors understand. IaC scanning integrates into CI/CD as a PR gate: new or modified infrastructure definitions are scanned on every pull request, and findings at or above a configured severity threshold block the merge. This is the IaC equivalent of SAST for application code — it catches coding-level mistakes before they reach any environment. At a more advanced level, drift detection tools compare deployed cloud state against the IaC definition to identify resources that were created or modified outside the IaC workflow.
words.connector: Think of IaC scanning like a building permit inspector who reviews architectural drawings before construction starts — catching a structural flaw in the blueprints costs far less than demolishing the building after it is built.
words.techContext: We run Checkov as a required PR gate on all Terraform PRs and have blocked over 200 misconfigured resources from reaching any environment, including 14 S3 buckets that would have been publicly accessible.
words.exampleSentence: The IaC scanning gate caught a Terraform module that granted the application role full S3 access to all buckets instead of the single target bucket, a least-privilege violation that would have been invisible in a traditional code review.

codeExample.code:
# GitHub Actions: Checkov IaC scan on Terraform PRs
jobs:
  checkov:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run Checkov
        uses: bridgecrewio/checkov-action@master
        with:
          directory: terraform/
          framework: terraform
          output_format: sarif
          output_file_path: checkov.sarif
          soft_fail: false        # fail the build on HIGH findings

      - name: Upload SARIF results
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: checkov.sarif

words.etymology: IaC (Infrastructure as Code) + scanning; IaC as a practice was popularized by HashiCorp Terraform (2014) and AWS CloudFormation (2011); security scanning for IaC emerged as a discipline around 2018–2020.

words.shortDefinition: Exploit Prediction Scoring System; probability score estimating the likelihood a CVE will be exploited in the wild.
words.simpleDefinition: EPSS gives each CVE a 0–1 probability of being exploited in the wild within the next 30 days, updated daily. A CVE with EPSS 0.94 has an estimated 94% chance of active exploitation. A high CVSS score with a low EPSS score (complex to exploit, no public tooling) should be deprioritized against a medium CVSS score with a high EPSS score that attackers are already using.
words.longDefinition: The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) was developed by the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) and is updated daily by a machine-learning model trained on over 1,500 features: CVE metadata, vulnerability type, affected software popularity, NVD descriptions, social media activity, exploit database entries, and observed exploitation telemetry from multiple threat intelligence feeds. EPSS v3 (released 2023) significantly improved accuracy over v1 and v2. The model outputs a probability score between 0.0 and 1.0: 0.94 means the model predicts a 94% chance that exploitation activity will be observed in the wild within 30 days. EPSS is complementary to CVSS, not a replacement. CVSS quantifies the intrinsic severity of a vulnerability if exploited; EPSS quantifies how likely exploitation is in practice. The combination is powerful for triage: CVSS Critical + EPSS 0.01 = high severity but very unlikely exploitation (low practical priority); CVSS Medium + EPSS 0.90 = moderate severity but active exploitation (high practical priority). Security teams use EPSS alongside the CISA KEV catalog to build dynamic, risk-ranked patch queues. SCA tools like Snyk and Grype integrate EPSS scores so that developers see exploitation probability alongside CVSS at the time of triaging findings, enabling evidence-based prioritization rather than severity-based flooding.
words.connector: Think of EPSS like a weather forecast for exploits: where CVSS tells you how destructive a storm could be, EPSS tells you the probability it will actually hit your area in the next 30 days.
words.techContext: After integrating EPSS into our SCA pipeline, we deprioritized 40% of our Critical-CVSS findings that had EPSS scores below 0.05 and fast-tracked three Medium-CVSS CVEs with EPSS scores above 0.85 that were already being exploited in the wild.
words.exampleSentence: The library's CVSS score was only 6.5, but its EPSS score of 0.97 meant it was one of the most actively exploited CVEs in the dataset — it jumped to the top of our patch queue immediately.

codeExample.code:
# Fetch EPSS score for a CVE via the FIRST API
CVE="CVE-2021-44228"   # Log4Shell
curl -s "https://api.first.org/data/1.0/epss?cve=${CVE}" \
  | jq '.data[] | {cve: .cve, epss: .epss, percentile: .percentile}'

# Example output:
# {
#   "cve": "CVE-2021-44228",
#   "epss": "0.97565",
#   "percentile": "0.99967"
# }
# → 97.6% probability of exploitation; 99.97th percentile of all CVEs

words.etymology: Acronym for Exploit Prediction Scoring System; developed by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) with academic partners; EPSS v1 published in 2019, v3 in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog; authoritative list of CVEs confirmed to be actively exploited.
words.simpleDefinition: The CISA KEV catalog is a curated, machine-readable list of CVEs that have been confirmed — not predicted — to be actively exploited against real targets. Federal agencies are legally required to patch KEV entries within specific deadlines. For everyone else, KEV is the most actionable signal for prioritizing vulnerability remediation: if a CVE is in KEV, attackers are using it right now.
words.longDefinition: The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog was launched by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency in November 2021 as a binding operational directive (BOD 22-01) for federal civilian agencies. Every CVE in the catalog has been confirmed by CISA to have active exploitation evidence — not theoretical risk, not EPSS probability, but observed real-world attacks. Federal agencies must remediate KEV entries within specified timeframes (typically 2 weeks for critical findings). The catalog is updated regularly and downloadable as a JSON feed. By Q2 2025 it contained approximately 1,200 entries, representing the curated highest-priority subset of the NVD's 200,000+ CVEs. KEV is intentionally small and actionable: the false positive rate approaches zero because entries require confirmed exploitation evidence. Security teams use KEV as the first filter in their patch queue: any CVE present in both the deployed SBOM and the KEV catalog is escalated to emergency patch status regardless of CVSS score. Tools like Grype, Trivy, and Dependency-Track can cross-reference SBOM findings against the KEV feed automatically. KEV also informs cyber insurance underwriting — several insurers now query applicants about KEV remediation cadence as part of risk assessment.
words.connector: Think of KEV like a most-wanted list: it is not a ranking of who is dangerous in theory, it is the confirmed list of vulnerabilities that criminals are actively using today.
words.techContext: Our SCA pipeline cross-references every SBOM against the CISA KEV JSON feed daily; a KEV hit on any production service triggers an automatic P0 incident and requires emergency patch deployment within 24 hours.
words.exampleSentence: Although the CVE had a CVSS score of only 5.8, its presence in the CISA KEV catalog meant it was being actively exploited in ransomware campaigns — it was patched within hours of discovery in our SBOM.

codeExample.code:
# Download KEV catalog and check if a CVE is listed
KEV_URL="https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json"
curl -s "$KEV_URL" \
  | jq --arg cve "CVE-2021-44228" \
    '.vulnerabilities[] | select(.cveID == $cve) | {cveID, vendorProject, product, requiredAction, dueDate}'

# Output:
# {
#   "cveID": "CVE-2021-44228",
#   "vendorProject": "Apache",
#   "product": "Log4j2",
#   "requiredAction": "Apply updates per vendor instructions.",
#   "dueDate": "2021-12-24"
# }

words.etymology: Acronym for Known Exploited Vulnerabilities; the catalog was established by CISA via Binding Operational Directive 22-01 issued on November 3, 2021.

words.shortDefinition: Common Vulnerability Scoring System; 0–10 numerical score rating the severity of a security vulnerability.
words.simpleDefinition: CVSS scores the inherent severity of a vulnerability — not your risk from it. A 9.8 score means that if this flaw is exploited against a vulnerable system, the impact is critical. It does not mean your system is at critical risk today; a critical CVE in software you do not run is irrelevant. The environmental score adjusts the base score for your actual exposure.
words.longDefinition: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) was developed by the National Infrastructure Advisory Council (NIAC) and is now maintained by FIRST. Version 3.1 is the most widely deployed; version 4.0 was released in 2023. CVSS has three metric groups: Base metrics capture the intrinsic properties of the vulnerability — Attack Vector (network/adjacent/local/physical), Attack Complexity (low/high), Privileges Required (none/low/high), User Interaction (none/required), Scope (unchanged/changed), and the CIA impact triad (None/Low/High for each of Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability). Base scores range from 0.0 to 10.0, with bands: Critical (9.0–10.0), High (7.0–8.9), Medium (4.0–6.9), Low (0.1–3.9), None (0.0). Temporal metrics adjust the score over time based on exploit code maturity (is there a public exploit?), remediation level (is a patch available?), and report confidence. Environmental metrics allow organizations to adjust for their specific deployment context: a CVSS 9.8 CVE in a library you do not ship, or that is not reachable from the internet, warrants a lower environmental score. The most important misunderstanding of CVSS is treating the base score as a risk score. CVSS measures severity; risk requires combining severity with exploitability (EPSS), actual exposure, and business impact. NVD (nvd.nist.gov) publishes base CVSS scores for all CVEs. CVSS was co-developed by Adam Shostack, who also wrote Threat Modeling: Designing for Security.
words.connector: Think of CVSS like a car crash test rating: a five-star crash test score tells you how bad an impact would be for an occupant, not how likely you are to crash. Risk requires knowing both the severity of the crash and the probability you are involved in one.
words.techContext: Our vulnerability triage policy uses CVSS to establish severity bands but pairs every Critical and High finding with EPSS and KEV lookup before scheduling remediation, preventing CVSS-score fatigue from flooding the patch queue.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration tester noted that the CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass was in a service only accessible from within our VPC — applying the environmental score adjusted the effective risk to 6.1, still High but no longer requiring emergency response.

codeExample.code:
# CVSS v3.1 vector string example (Log4Shell)
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H

# Decoded:
# AV:N   = Attack Vector: Network (remotely exploitable)
# AC:L   = Attack Complexity: Low (no special conditions)
# PR:N   = Privileges Required: None
# UI:N   = User Interaction: None
# S:C    = Scope: Changed (can affect other components)
# C:H    = Confidentiality Impact: High
# I:H    = Integrity Impact: High
# A:H    = Availability Impact: High

# Base score: 10.0 (Critical)
# Environmental score (library not in external-facing service): 5.9 (Medium)

words.etymology: Acronym for Common Vulnerability Scoring System; developed by the NIAC in 2004, transferred to FIRST in 2005; v3.1 released 2019, v4.0 released 2023.

words.shortDefinition: Automated detection of hardcoded credentials, API keys, and tokens committed to source control repositories.
words.simpleDefinition: Secrets scanning detects credentials — API keys, database passwords, private keys, OAuth tokens — that developers accidentally commit to Git. Pre-commit hooks block the commit locally; PR-level scanning blocks the merge; repository-wide scanning finds historical secrets already committed. A credential found in a repo should be treated as compromised and rotated immediately, regardless of repo visibility.
words.longDefinition: Secrets scanning is a category of automated security tooling that applies pattern matching and entropy analysis to source code, commit history, and code review diffs to detect credentials before or immediately after they are committed. Common detected secret types include API keys (AWS, GCP, Azure, Stripe, Twilio), database connection strings, RSA/ECDSA private keys, OAuth tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, SSH keys, and JWT signing secrets. Tooling spans three deployment points: pre-commit hooks (Gitleaks, detect-secrets, TruffleHog) run locally before a commit is recorded; CI/CD integration (GitHub Advanced Security, GitLab Secret Detection, Gitleaks GitHub Action) blocks PRs before merge; and continuous repository scanning (GitHub secret scanning, GitLab, Truffles) monitors the full history including previously merged commits and surfaces alerts for newly added pattern definitions. GitHub's secret scanning program (launched 2018) includes a partner program where token issuers (AWS, Stripe, etc.) register their key format; GitHub notifies the provider when a matching pattern is found and the provider immediately revokes the credential. Private repository scanning is included in GitHub Advanced Security. The critical operational rule is that any committed secret must be treated as compromised and rotated immediately, even in a private repository with immediate deletion — the credential may have been logged, cached, or observed before deletion.
words.connector: Think of secrets scanning like a metal detector at a loading dock — it does not prevent smuggling entirely, but it catches most contraband before it crosses the perimeter, and it keeps the loading crew honest.
words.techContext: After enabling Gitleaks as a pre-commit hook and in CI, we caught a developer accidentally committing a Stripe test API key in a config file — the secret was rotated before the commit ever reached the remote repository.
words.exampleSentence: The repository audit found a production AWS key committed in a Dockerfile two years earlier, still active and with full S3 write permissions — secrets scanning with historical scanning would have surfaced this the day it was committed.

codeExample.code:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml: Gitleaks secret scanning hook
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

# GitHub Actions: scan on every PR
- name: Gitleaks secret scan
  uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
  env:
    GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    GITLEAKS_LICENSE: ${{ secrets.GITLEAKS_LICENSE }}
  with:
    args: --baseline-path gitleaks-report.json

words.etymology: Compound of 'secrets' (sensitive credentials) + 'scanning' (automated inspection); as a named security discipline, popularized with the launch of GitHub's secret scanning feature in 2018 and the growth of pre-commit tooling.

words.shortDefinition: Compromise that targets a dependency, build tool, or distribution channel to reach many downstream victims at once.
words.simpleDefinition: A supply chain attack does not target your application directly — it targets something your application trusts: a popular open-source library, your CI build system, a code signing key, or a software update server. By compromising one link, the attacker automatically reaches every downstream consumer who installs the update or imports the library.
words.longDefinition: A software supply chain attack exploits the trust relationships in the software development and distribution pipeline. Instead of attacking a hardened production system directly, adversaries find a weaker link upstream: a widely-used open-source library, a CI/CD system, a build pipeline, a package registry, or a software update mechanism. Compromising that link gives the attacker automatic access to every system that depends on it. The 2020 SolarWinds attack is the canonical example: Russian state-sponsored actors (APT29/Cozy Bear) compromised SolarWinds' Orion build pipeline, injecting the SUNBURST backdoor into a signed software update shipped to approximately 18,000 organizations including US federal agencies, Microsoft, and FireEye. The artifact was signed with SolarWinds' legitimate certificate, making signature verification useless. The 2024 xz-utils incident demonstrated a patience-based variant: a threat actor spent approximately two years contributing legitimately to the xz-utils project under the identity 'JiaT75', building trust, eventually becoming a maintainer, then inserting a backdoor into the build system (not the source) targeting SSH authentication on select Linux distributions. Supply chain attacks are highly asymmetric: compromising one maintainer account or one build system yields access to millions of downstream installations simultaneously. Defenses include SBOM generation, SLSA provenance attestations, IaC scanning, secrets scanning, dependency pinning with integrity hashes, and private artifact proxies with allowlists.
words.connector: Think of a supply chain attack like contaminating a city's water supply rather than poisoning individual households: one upstream compromise reaches every consumer who trusts the tap.
words.techContext: After the xz-utils incident our security team audited all packages with elevated install-time privileges in our CI environment, added Cosign signature verification to our Docker base image pulls, and implemented SLSA Level 2 provenance for all first-party artifacts.
words.exampleSentence: The SolarWinds attack demonstrated that a signed, widely-trusted software update is not sufficient proof of integrity — the signing key itself, and the build pipeline that produced the artifact, must also be protected.

codeExample.code:
# Supply chain attack surface map — layers to defend:

1. Source code          → signed commits, branch protection, 2FA on developer accounts
2. Dependencies         → lockfiles, integrity hashes, SCA scanning, allowlist proxy
3. Build tools          → pinned tool versions, hermetic build environments
4. Build pipeline       → SLSA Level 2+, least-privilege CI permissions, secrets scanning
5. Build outputs        → SBOM generation, Cosign signing, provenance attestation
6. Distribution         → signed packages, Sigstore/Rekor transparency log
7. Deployment           → provenance verification at admission, Cosign policy-controller

# Each layer addresses a specific attack vector from the SolarWinds / xz pattern

words.etymology: Borrowed from manufacturing supply chain management; in information security the term describes attacks on the software development and distribution pipeline; popularized after the SolarWinds incident in December 2020.

words.shortDefinition: 2020 nation-state compromise of SolarWinds build pipeline; malicious code signed and shipped to 18,000 customers.
words.simpleDefinition: In late 2020, Russian state actors compromised SolarWinds' Orion software build pipeline and injected the SUNBURST backdoor into an update shipped to approximately 18,000 organizations. Because the artifact was signed with SolarWinds' legitimate certificate, standard security controls — signature verification, antivirus — did not detect it. Victims included US federal agencies, Microsoft, Intel, and Cisco.
words.longDefinition: The SolarWinds attack (publicly disclosed December 13, 2020) is the most consequential software supply chain attack in history and the event that made supply-chain security a board-level concern. Russian-state-affiliated threat actors, identified as Cozy Bear (APT29), gained access to SolarWinds' build environment and implanted the SUNBURST backdoor into the Orion IT monitoring platform's build process. The malicious code was dormant for two weeks after installation to evade sandbox analysis, then established a covert communication channel to attacker-controlled infrastructure using steganographically encoded DNS traffic. The artifact was built by SolarWinds' legitimate build system and signed with SolarWinds' authentic code-signing certificate, making it indistinguishable from legitimate updates. Approximately 18,000 SolarWinds customers installed the malicious update; of those, around 100 were subsequently actively exploited for lateral movement, data exfiltration, and persistent access. Victims included the US Departments of Treasury, Commerce, Homeland Security, State, and Justice; Microsoft; Intel; Cisco; and the cybersecurity firm FireEye (whose discovery triggered the public disclosure). The attack exploited the implicit trust that 'signed artifact from a known vendor equals safe' — a trust that SLSA, Sigstore, and provenance attestations are specifically designed to make falsifiable. The SUNBURST payload sat in Orion updates versions 2019.4 through 2020.2.1 and remained undetected for approximately nine months.
words.connector: Think of the SolarWinds attack like a trusted postal carrier delivering a package that had been secretly replaced during sorting — every address on the delivery route received the attacker's payload, and the authentic tracking label on the box gave no indication anything was wrong.
words.techContext: The SolarWinds attack is the canonical justification for SLSA provenance attestations: even a legitimate build system producing signed artifacts is insufficient if the build pipeline itself can be compromised; attestations that record and sign the exact build inputs and environment make such tampering detectable.
words.exampleSentence: The SolarWinds attack taught the industry that a valid code signature proves only that the signer had access to the signing key — it says nothing about whether the build pipeline that produced the artifact was itself trustworthy.

codeExample.code:
# Timeline: SolarWinds SUNBURST attack

Oct 2019  : Attackers compromise SolarWinds build environment
Mar 2020  : SUNBURST backdoor injected into Orion build pipeline
Mar–Jun   : Trojanized Orion updates (2019.4–2020.2.1) signed and distributed
            ~18,000 organizations install the malicious update
Jun 2020  : Attackers activate backdoor in ~100 high-value targets
Dec 13    : FireEye publicly discloses SUNBURST after discovering it in their network
Dec 14    : CISA Emergency Directive 21-01: all agencies disconnect SolarWinds Orion

Control failures:
  - Build pipeline integrity not monitored
  - No provenance attestation (attacker modified the build, not the source)
  - Signed artifact trusted implicitly without verifying build provenance

Controls that would have helped:
  - SLSA Level 3+ (hardened build environment)
  - Reproducible builds (compare distributed vs. independently built artifact)

words.etymology: SolarWinds is the name of the affected software vendor; attack describes the supply-chain compromise; named as the SolarWinds attack or SUNBURST (the malware name) in industry literature; publicly disclosed December 2020.

words.shortDefinition: Vulnerability scanning of container images for known CVEs in OS packages and application dependencies.
words.simpleDefinition: Container scanning inspects a Docker or OCI image layer by layer, extracting the package manifest from the base OS and any application dependency managers, then matching every installed package against CVE databases. It catches vulnerabilities in the base image (e.g., a vulnerable glibc in ubuntu:22.04) and in your application's dependencies (e.g., a vulnerable log4j JAR inside the image), before the image is ever deployed.
words.longDefinition: Container scanning is a form of software composition analysis (SCA) applied to OCI-format container images. Scanners like Trivy, Grype, Snyk Container, Clair, and Amazon Inspector extract the bill of materials from a container image by parsing the layer filesystem: they enumerate OS packages (dpkg, rpm, apk), language runtime dependencies (pip requirements, npm lock files, Maven POMs, Go module cache), and sometimes application binaries. Each detected component is cross-referenced against CVE databases: NVD, GitHub Advisory Database, distro-specific advisories (Debian Security, Red Hat Security, Ubuntu Security Notices), and language-ecosystem advisories (PyPA, GitHub npm advisories). Findings include the CVE identifier, affected component, installed version, fixed version if available, CVSS score, and EPSS score. Container scanning integrates at multiple pipeline stages: as a CI gate (block image push if any Critical/High CVEs exceed the threshold), as a registry-side scan (cloud registries like Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, and GitHub Container Registry scan images on push), and as a continuous runtime scan (Trivy Operator, Starboard) that monitors running images against newly published CVEs. Scanning base images regularly is equally important as scanning application layers: a 'latest' base image pulled six months ago may contain dozens of unpatched OS vulnerabilities. Best practice is to pin base images to digests (not tags) and run container scanning on every PR that modifies the Dockerfile.
words.connector: Think of container scanning like a customs inspector who opens every shipping container and checks each item inside against a list of banned goods — not just the manifest the shipper provided.
words.techContext: Our CI pipeline runs Trivy on every container image build with --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL, blocking pushes to the registry when any critical OS or application CVE is found that has an available fix.
words.exampleSentence: Container scanning surfaced a critical OpenSSL CVE in the base image we had pinned three months earlier; without the scan, we would have shipped a container with a known-exploited vulnerability to all production replicas.

codeExample.code:
# GitHub Actions: Trivy container scan before push
- name: Build image
  run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

- name: Scan image for CVEs
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
    format: sarif
    output: trivy-results.sarif
    severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    exit-code: 1          # fail the build on findings
    ignore-unfixed: true  # skip CVEs with no available fix

- name: Upload scan results
  uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
  if: always()
  with:
    sarif_file: trivy-results.sarif

words.etymology: Container from the Docker container metaphor (a standardized unit of software); scanning from automated inspection; as a security practice, emerged with the adoption of Docker in production environments (2014–2016) and the growth of container-specific CVE databases.

words.shortDefinition: Security and compliance rules expressed as machine-executable code (e.g., OPA Rego) and enforced in CI/CD pipelines.
words.simpleDefinition: Policy as Code replaces security rules that exist only in documents with executable code checked into version control. Policies like 'all containers must run as non-root', 'all S3 buckets must have encryption enabled', or 'no Critical CVEs in production images' are written in a policy language (OPA Rego, Kyverno YAML, Sentinel) and enforced automatically — in CI, in Kubernetes admission controllers, or in cloud provisioning workflows.
words.longDefinition: Policy as Code (PaC) applies the Infrastructure as Code discipline to governance: instead of a Word document that a human must interpret, enforce, and periodically review, a policy is expressed as code that can be version-controlled, peer-reviewed, tested, and executed automatically. The benefits are identical to IaC: git history of all policy changes, code review for policy modifications, unit tests for policy rules, and consistent enforcement. In the Kubernetes ecosystem, OPA (Open Policy Agent) with Rego and Kyverno are the two dominant engines. OPA is a general-purpose policy engine: you write Rego rules that accept JSON input and return allow/deny, then configure the OPA admission webhook to intercept all Kubernetes API requests. Kyverno uses a more declarative Kubernetes-native syntax in YAML, making it more approachable for teams that want to avoid learning Rego. In CI/CD, Checkov enforces IaC policies on Terraform and CloudFormation; conftest (also using Rego) tests Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, and Dockerfiles; HashiCorp Sentinel enforces policies in Terraform Cloud. GitHub's required workflows act as PaC at the organization level: every repository must run specific security scan workflows before merging. Policy drift — policies that exist in documents but are inconsistently enforced — is a leading cause of audit failures; PaC eliminates drift by making enforcement continuous, auditable, and automatically applied to every resource creation or modification.
words.connector: Think of Policy as Code like traffic enforcement cameras: instead of relying on police to be present at every intersection, the policy is expressed in the camera's software and enforced automatically on every car that passes.
words.techContext: We use Kyverno in our Kubernetes clusters to enforce that all pods have resource limits set, all images are pulled from our approved registry and carry a Cosign signature, and no container runs with privileged: true.
words.exampleSentence: After shifting our security controls to policy as code in Kyverno, an engineer who tried to deploy a privileged pod for debugging was blocked by the admission controller before the workload could start, with a clear policy violation message explaining the rule.

codeExample.code:
# Kyverno policy: require non-root containers and resource limits
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-non-root-with-limits
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: check-non-root
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Pod]
      validate:
        message: "Containers must not run as root and must have resource limits."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - securityContext:
                  runAsNonRoot: true
                resources:
                  limits:
                    memory: "?*"
                    cpu: "?*"

words.etymology: Analogy to Infrastructure as Code; popularized alongside the rise of OPA (Open Policy Agent, CNCF project, accepted 2018) and Kyverno; the phrase 'Policy as Code' was in broad use by 2019–2020.

words.shortDefinition: Moving security testing as close as possible to code creation — IDE plugins, pre-commit hooks, PR gates — to cut remediation cost.
words.simpleDefinition: Shift-left security means running security checks at the earliest possible stage: IDE plugins while you type, pre-commit hooks before a commit lands, PR gates before code merges. The later a security flaw is found — staging, pen test, production incident — the more it costs to fix. A flaw caught in the IDE costs minutes; the same flaw found in production costs days and may require customer notification.
words.longDefinition: Shift-left security draws its name from the software development pipeline visualized as a left-to-right timeline: commit → build → test → security → deploy → operate. Moving security checks to the left — earlier — reduces the cost of finding and remediating flaws exponentially. NIST data suggests a production defect costs 15× more to fix than one found during development; for security vulnerabilities the multiplier is larger because production exposure can trigger incident response, credential rotation, regulatory disclosure, and customer notification. The shift-left security stack, ordered from leftmost to rightmost: IDE plugins (Snyk, SonarLint, Semgrep) surface findings as the developer types; pre-commit hooks (Gitleaks, detect-secrets, Semgrep) block commits containing secrets or known-vulnerable code patterns; pull-request gates run full SAST (Semgrep, CodeQL) and SCA (Snyk, Dependabot) scans and block merges on Critical/High findings; post-merge scans run full repository-wide analysis; scheduled deep scans cover newly disclosed CVEs against the deployed SBOM. The cultural dimension of shift-left is as important as the tooling: developers must own security findings in their code, not hand them off to a separate security team that operates as a gateway. Security engineers' role shifts from approvers to enablers — building shared policy libraries, training developers, and reviewing escalated findings — rather than being the sole responsible party for every finding.
words.connector: Think of shift-left security like catching a typo during a phone call rather than after the contract is printed, signed, and sent to the client — the same information caught 10 minutes earlier costs nothing to fix.
words.techContext: After deploying Semgrep as an IDE plugin and a PR gate, the average time from vulnerability introduction to detection dropped from 18 days (when quarterly pen tests were our primary detection) to under 4 minutes.
words.exampleSentence: Shift-left security moved our SQL injection detection from a quarterly penetration test — where findings averaged 6 weeks to remediate — to a PR gate that blocks the commit within 90 seconds of push.

codeExample.code:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml: shift-left security hooks
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks           # secrets scanning

  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v4.5.0
    hooks:
      - id: detect-private-key # private key detection
      - id: check-merge-conflict

  - repo: https://github.com/returntocorp/semgrep
    rev: v1.52.0
    hooks:
      - id: semgrep
        args: ['--config', 'p/owasp-top-ten', '--error']

words.etymology: Shift-left refers to moving activities toward the left on the classic software development lifecycle diagram; as a security term, popularized in the 2010s alongside the DevSecOps movement.

words.shortDefinition: Signed metadata documenting the source, build inputs, and build process that produced a software artifact.
words.simpleDefinition: A provenance attestation is a cryptographically signed receipt that answers: what source code was built, on which platform, by which process, and at which time? Stored alongside the artifact in an OCI registry or transparency log, it lets consumers verify a container image or binary was produced by an official CI workflow from a specific commit — not by a compromised developer machine or a modified fork.
words.longDefinition: Provenance attestations are the cornerstone of software supply-chain integrity. The in-toto attestation framework (developed at NYU, in-toto.io) defines the envelope format: a signed JSON document with a statement type (the kind of claim being made), a subject (the artifact being attested, identified by digest), and a predicate (the claims themselves). SLSA provenance is the most widely adopted predicate type and records: builder identity (the URI of the build platform, e.g., GitHub Actions), build type (the schema of the build process), invocation (the workflow file and git ref that triggered the build), materials (the source commit SHA and transitive inputs), and the timestamp of the build. Attestations are stored as OCI artifacts in the same registry as the image (via Cosign attest) or appended to a transparency log (Rekor). Consumers use cosign verify-attestation or the gh attestation verify command to retrieve and check attestations against a policy: 'this image must have been built from github.com/myorg/myrepo by the official release.yml workflow on refs/heads/main'. Kubernetes admission controllers (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper with Ratify, sigstore policy-controller) can enforce provenance policies as deployment gates — rejecting any image that cannot produce a valid attestation matching the cluster's policy. The SolarWinds and xz-utils attacks both modified the build process, not the tracked source; provenance attestations recording and signing the build environment would have made those modifications detectable by downstream consumers.
words.connector: Think of a provenance attestation like a chain of custody form for physical evidence: it records every hand that touched the artifact and every step in its journey from source to production, with each step cryptographically signed by the party who performed it.
words.techContext: Our Kubernetes admission controller uses Ratify + OPA to require that every container image in the production namespace carry a valid SLSA provenance attestation signed by the GitHub Actions workflow identity of our official release pipeline before the pod is admitted.
words.exampleSentence: The provenance attestation on the suspicious image showed it had been built from a fork rather than the official repository — the deviation was detectable in seconds and immediately identified the injection point in the supply chain.
words.etymology: Provenance from Old French provenance ('origin, source'); attestation from Latin attestari ('to bear witness to'); the compound term was formalized in the in-toto framework and SLSA specification documents circa 2021.

words.shortDefinition: Hierarchical diagram representing an attacker's goal at the root and all possible paths to achieve it as branches.
words.simpleDefinition: An attack tree starts with the attacker's goal at the top — 'steal user credentials', 'exfiltrate the database', 'gain admin access' — and decomposes it into sub-goals and atomic steps below. OR nodes mean any one child path is sufficient; AND nodes mean all child paths must succeed. The tree makes multi-step attack paths explicit and can be annotated with cost, likelihood, and skill required at each leaf.
words.longDefinition: Attack trees were introduced by Bruce Schneier in a December 1999 article in Dr. Dobb's Journal, adapted from fault trees used in safety engineering. The root node represents the attacker's high-level goal. Internal nodes represent sub-goals, connected by AND or OR logic: an OR node means achieving any one child sub-goal is sufficient to achieve the parent; an AND node means all child sub-goals must be achieved (a prerequisite chain). Leaf nodes represent atomic, observable attack steps. Leaf nodes can be annotated with attacker attributes that propagate up the tree: cost (in dollars or time), skill required (script kiddie vs. nation-state), probability of success, and detectability. These attributes combine mathematically — OR costs take the minimum (attacker picks the cheapest path); AND costs sum (all steps must be done). The result is a composite cost-and-likelihood estimate for each attack path, enabling rational prioritization of defenses: invest in controls that block the most likely or cheapest path to the goal. Attack trees complement STRIDE: STRIDE generates a categorized threat list; attack trees model specific multi-step attack paths for the highest-priority threats in detail. MITRE ATT&CK (attack.mitre.org) provides a knowledge base of real-world attacker TTPs that populate leaf nodes with empirically observed techniques rather than hypothetical ones. Tools like SeaSponge (open source), AttackTree+, and IriusRisk support attack tree construction.
words.connector: Think of an attack tree like a flowchart for burglars planning to rob a house: the goal is at the top, and every branch below represents a different way to get in — picking the lock, breaking a window, or tricking a resident. AND means they need all the steps; OR means any one will do.
words.techContext: During our PASTA threat modeling session for the payments API, we built attack trees for the top two STRIDE threats — credential theft and payment amount manipulation — and discovered that the cheapest path to credential theft required only a phishing email, not a technical exploit.
words.exampleSentence: The attack tree for 'gain admin access to the admin console' revealed that the cheapest attack path cost less than $50 in social engineering tools, compared to $50,000 for a zero-day exploit — the risk decision became obvious.

words.shortDefinition: Diagram showing how data moves between processes, data stores, and external entities; used to locate trust boundaries.
words.simpleDefinition: A data flow diagram (DFD) is the primary artifact of threat modeling. It maps four element types — external entities, processes, data stores, and data flows — and draws explicit lines where data crosses trust boundaries. Every arrow crossing a trust boundary is a potential vulnerability: it is a point where one party's data enters another party's control without validation.
words.longDefinition: Data Flow Diagrams originated in structured systems analysis (DeMarco, 1979) and were adopted into security threat modeling by Microsoft's SDL practice. A DFD uses four standardized element types: external entities (rectangles) — actors outside the system boundary: browsers, mobile apps, third-party APIs, human users; processes (circles or rounded boxes) — code that transforms data: web servers, microservices, Lambda functions; data stores (parallel lines) — places data rests: databases, caches, file systems, message queues; data flows (arrows) — movement of data between elements, labeled with the data type and protocol. Trust boundaries are drawn as dashed lines separating zones of different trust: the Internet/DMZ boundary, the DMZ/internal boundary, the application/database boundary, the user context/admin context boundary. Every data flow crossing a trust boundary is a mandatory inspection point. DFDs are drawn at two levels of detail: Level 0 (context diagram — the entire system as a single process surrounded by external actors) and Level 1 (individual services and data stores expanded). Security threat modeling operates primarily at Level 1. A DFD drawn before a design review is more valuable than any number of post-deployment security audits because it forces explicit agreement about what the system does, who controls which data, and where validation is required. The question 'who is responsible for validating data at this trust boundary crossing?' must have a concrete answer for every arrow that crosses a boundary line.
words.connector: Think of a DFD like a subway map for your data: the stations are your processes and data stores, the tracks are the data flows, and the zone boundaries are your trust boundaries — every time data crosses from one zone to another it should go through a checkpoint.
words.techContext: Drawing the Level 1 DFD for our new file-upload feature revealed that we had three trust boundary crossings without explicit validation: user input to virus scanner, virus scanner output to storage service, and storage service metadata to the database query.
words.exampleSentence: The DFD exposed a data flow we had forgotten entirely: the nightly export job moved PII from the production database across the internal/DMZ trust boundary to an unencrypted S3 bucket with public-read permissions.

words.shortDefinition: Runtime Application Self-Protection; agent embedded in production that detects and blocks attacks in real time.
words.simpleDefinition: RASP is an agent running inside your application process — not in front of it like a WAF. It instruments the application at the bytecode or library level to observe exactly what the code is about to do: execute a SQL query, spawn a shell, read a file. If the operation looks malicious based on the current request context, RASP blocks the call and logs the attack attempt from inside the process.
words.longDefinition: Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) was coined by Gartner analyst Joseph Feiman in 2012. A RASP agent is typically injected into the application via a language-level hook: Java agents (JVMTI), .NET profiler API, Python import hooks, or Node.js module patching. The agent intercepts critical operations at runtime — SQL query execution, OS command invocation, file system access, XML parsing, HTTP outbound calls — and evaluates them against the current HTTP request context. If a SQL string being executed contains user-supplied input in a structural position (e.g., closing a quoted string), RASP blocks the execution and raises an alert. RASP's primary advantage over a WAF is that it operates inside the application with full awareness of the execution context: it can distinguish between a legitimate admin action and an attack more accurately than a network-layer proxy. RASP cannot be bypassed by encoding tricks that fool network-level WAFs because it inspects the decoded, deserialized operation just before execution. Common RASP vendors include Sqreen (acquired by Datadog), Contrast Security, Dynatrace Application Security, and Imperva RASP. RASP is not a testing tool — it is a production defense layer. It is commonly confused with IAST because both instrument the running application; IAST runs during automated testing in non-production environments, while RASP runs in production and actively blocks attacks.
words.connector: Think of RASP like a surgeon's assistant who can grab the surgeon's hand mid-operation and say 'that cut would hit an artery' — it intercepts and stops the dangerous action from inside the process, just before the harm occurs.
words.techContext: After deploying a RASP agent on our Java API service, we observed three SQL injection attempts per day being blocked automatically — none had been detected by our WAF because the payloads used unicode normalization to bypass its pattern matching.
words.exampleSentence: The RASP agent blocked a second-order SQL injection attempt that our input validation had missed — the payload was stored at registration time and only became injected SQL when re-read six hours later during a report generation job.
words.etymology: Acronym for Runtime Application Self-Protection; coined by Gartner analyst Joseph Feiman in 2012 to describe the emerging category of in-process security agents that protect applications from within.

words.shortDefinition: Memory-hard key derivation function designed to be costly for ASIC-based cracking; alternative to Argon2.
words.simpleDefinition: scrypt makes password cracking expensive by requiring large amounts of RAM in addition to CPU time. An ASIC built to crack bcrypt hashes at high speed cannot be applied to scrypt without enormous memory per core, which massively limits parallelism. It is the second-choice KDF after Argon2id for environments where Argon2 is unavailable, and the algorithm behind the Litecoin and Dogecoin proof-of-work schemes.
words.longDefinition: scrypt was designed by Colin Percival and published in 2009 specifically to defend against commodity hardware attacks on password hashes. At the time, bcrypt was the best widely-available password hashing function, but its memory requirements were minimal — allowing attackers to build or buy GPUs and ASICs that could compute billions of bcrypt hashes per second in parallel. scrypt introduced the concept of memory-hardness: the algorithm is parameterized with N (CPU/memory cost factor), r (block size), and p (parallelism factor) and requires N × r × 128 bytes of working memory per hash. A typical production configuration of N=2^17, r=8, p=1 requires 128 MB of RAM per hash attempt. An ASIC optimized for scrypt needs 128 MB of RAM per parallel hash lane, making a 10,000-lane ASIC impossible — it would require 1.28 TB of RAM. scrypt is the algorithm powering Litecoin's proof-of-work and was added to PKCS#5 (RFC 7914). For password hashing specifically, Argon2id is now preferred because it is the PHC winner (2015) and has better-understood security properties. scrypt is the appropriate choice when Argon2 is unavailable (older cryptographic libraries, FIPS environments where Argon2 has not been approved) and bcrypt/PBKDF2 are insufficient. All password-hashing KDFs — Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt — must be configured with work factors that make each hash attempt take approximately 100–300ms on current hardware.
words.connector: Think of scrypt like a combination lock that requires not just time to spin the dials but also a key that takes up half a filing cabinet — you can't speed it up by having more hands because each hand still needs the cabinet.
words.techContext: We use scrypt via libsodium's crypto_pwhash_scryptsalsa208sha256 with N=2^17 on our legacy authentication service while we migrate to Argon2id; both algorithms meet OWASP's memory-hardness recommendations.
words.exampleSentence: The security audit recommended replacing the PBKDF2 configuration in the legacy auth module with scrypt or Argon2id, noting that PBKDF2's lack of memory-hardness made it vulnerable to GPU-accelerated offline cracking in a credential-stuffing scenario.
